Soil sampling, testing, analysis and issue of soil test report to farmers along with crop specific recommendation of fertilizers based on soil test outcome has been a mandate of the Department of Agriculture. From the year -2012 onwards soil test reports were given in a comprehensive manner as Farmers Integrated Handbook. From the year 2014-2015 onwards Soil Health Card (SHC) scheme was introduced under National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, a centrally sponsored scheme under which support for soil sampling, analysis and printing of soil health cards was given. Soil Health Card is a semi-permanent record with a validity period of three years. The Soil Health Card scheme has been merged with Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) from the year 2023-2024.

2. The main objective of issuing Soil Health Card is to promote Integrated Nutrient Management through judicious use of chemical fertilizers including secondary and micro nutrients in conjunction with organic manures, bio fertilizers for improving soil health and ultimately the crop productivity.

3. Tamil Nadu soils are low in Organic Carbon and Nitrogen content, medium in Phosphorus content, high in Potassium content. With respect to Micronutrients, they are deficient in Zinc and Copper, sufficient in Sulphur, Boron, Manganese and Iron. Understanding soil fertility and to practice judicious use of fertilizers by farmers in the field is essential to

maintain soil health.

[P.t.o]

2

4. In pursuit of higher production, there is a tendency among farmers to use fertilizers and pesticides over and above the actual requirement leading to depletion of soil health, particularly, reduced microbial activity in the soil. It is also an established fact that excess chemical usage is one of the causes for many pest and diseases. There is a need to adopt soil test based balanced use of fertilizers by integrating bio/organic fertilizers into agriculture for nutritional security of soil. There are many traditional practices like application of botanicals, organic manuring etc that have to be revisited and embraced in a large scale without compromising on the production.

Ref: G.O.(Ms).No.113, Housing and Urban Development [UD1(2)] Department, dated 22.6.2017. The real estate sector has grown rapidly in the recent years and from the perspective of consumer protection, the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 has been enacted.

2. Some of the salient features of the Act are as follows:-

a. Establishment of on Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA) in every State in India for monitoring and adjudicating disputes relating to real estate projects (Section 20).

b. Establishment of fast track dispute resolution mechanism for settlement of real estate disputes through dedicated adjudicating officers and Appellate Tribunal (Section 43 & 44).

You may keep note of this aspect in making your suggestion.

9. Iam therefore to request you to nominate / suggest list of suitable experts in the field of Urban development, Housing Real Estate development, Infrastructure, Economics, Planning, Law, Commerce, Accountancy, Industry, Management, Public affairs or administration and possess experience of atleast twenty years in the field or who has held the post in the Central Government, or a State Government equivalent to the post of Additional Secretary to the Government of India or an equivalent post in the Central Government or an equivalent post in the State Government.

2.a.Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women (TNCDW)

The Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women (TNCDW) was established in 1983 by the Government of Tamil Nadu with the Primary objective of social and economic empowerment of women through education, employment, economic development and self-reliance.

The Self-Help Group (SHG) movement in Tamil Nadu was nurtured by TNCDW for the overall development of rural women by instilling a sense of bonding and confidence through a wide range of capacity building activities and forming Cammunity Based Organizations (CBOs) like the Panchayat Level Federations (PLFs), Block Level Federations (BLFs), etc. and facilitating bank credit for income generation through economic activities and various poverty alleviation programmes.

A total of 3.95 lakhs SHGs are active in rural and urban areas of Tamil Nadu. In addition to this, SHGs are also formed and Supported by various Government and Non-Government Organisations (NGOs),

2.b. Self Help Group (SHG) Movement

The seeds of the Self Help Group (SHG) concept for the Socio-economic empowerment of women was sown in 1989 at Dharmapuri. The SHG concept gained momentum under International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) assisted project and with the introduction of the Mahalir Thittam in 1996, it was slowly extended to other districts and by the year 2000, all districts including Chennai

13

District was included under the scheme. Due to the strong SHG base created in the State, the Swarnaajayanthi Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) a Centrally Sponsored Scheme launched in 1999 to address rural poverty with focus on SHG was effectively implemented for economic improvement of the rural poor. During the year 2022-2023, 4,39,349 SHGs have been assisted with a credit linkage of Rs.25,022.19 crore with an average loan size per SHG is Rs.5.68 lakh.

2.c. Poverty Alleviation and Livelihood Missions

The Government of Tamil Nadu is a model welfare State which focuses on inclusive socio-economic development through multivarious schemes that provide opportunities for disadvantaged people to access the benefits of programmes and projects and improve their quality of life. The Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department is vested with the important mandate of poverty alleviation and socio-economic empowerment of the poor, marginalized and vulnerable families through livelihood promotion programmes anchored by the Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women and the World Bank assisted “Yaazhndhu Kaattuvom” Project now continued as Tamil Nadu Rural Transformation Project.

2.1 Agriculture and Allied Sectors

In Tamil Nadu, majority of economically productive women are engaged as agricultural labourers. Despite their large presence and contribution to rural economy, their work is limited to less skilled jobs such as sowing, transplanting, weeding, harvesting etc. Further, Women cultivators are very less in number and do not have proper access to inputs (seed, fertilizer), credit facility, organised markets, advanced technologies such as use of drudgery reduction technologies etc. The State shall therefore take necessary measures to support women in agriculture.

ABSTRACT Agriculture - Farmers Welfare - Soil Health Card based fertilizer recommendations - recommendation of organic manures, bio fertilizers in the Soil Health Card - To be specified - Orders - Issued.

AGRICULTURE - FARMERS WELFARE (AP4) DEPARTMENT

G.O. (Ms) No.263 Dated:07.11.2024 @CorS) aH, guu 21, Slapoucit oot 2, c0d0r(h| 2055 Read:

1. G.O.(Ms) No. 185, Agriculture-Farmers Welfare (AP4) Department, dated 14.08.2024.

2. Minutes of the Review meeting Chaired by the Hon’ble Minister for Agriculture - Farmers Welfare on 12.09.2024.

ORDER:

Soil sampling, testing, analysis and issue of soil test report to farmers along with crop specific recommendation of fertilizers based on soil test outcome has been a mandate of the Department of Agriculture. From the year -2012 onwards soil test reports were given in a comprehensive manner as Farmers Integrated Handbook. From the year 2014-2015 onwards Soil Health Card (SHC) scheme was introduced under National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, a centrally sponsored scheme under which support for soil sampling, analysis and printing of soil health cards was given. Soil Health Card is a semi-permanent record with a validity period of three years. The Soil Health Card scheme has been merged with Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) from the year 2023-2024.

2. The main objective of issuing Soil Health Card is to promote Integrated Nutrient Management through judicious use of chemical fertilizers including secondary and micro nutrients in conjunction with organic manures, bio fertilizers for improving soil health and ultimately the crop productivity.

3. Tamil Nadu soils are low in Organic Carbon and Nitrogen content, medium in Phosphorus content, high in Potassium content. With respect to Micronutrients, they are deficient in Zinc and Copper, sufficient in Sulphur, Boron, Manganese and Iron. Understanding soil fertility and to practice judicious use of fertilizers by farmers in the field is essential to

maintain soil health.

[P.t.o]

2

4. In pursuit of higher production, there is a tendency among farmers to use fertilizers and pesticides over and above the actual requirement leading to depletion of soil health, particularly, reduced microbial activity in the soil. It is also an established fact that excess chemical usage is one of the causes for many pest and diseases. There is a need to adopt soil test based balanced use of fertilizers by integrating bio/organic fertilizers into agriculture for nutritional security of soil. There are many traditional practices like application of botanicals, organic manuring etc that have to be revisited and embraced in a large scale without compromising on the production.
